12: # Cybersecurity Analyst Skill
13: 
14: ## Purpose
15: 
16: Analyze events through the disciplinary lens of cybersecurity, applying rigorous security frameworks (CIA triad, defense-in-depth, zero-trust), threat modeling methodologies (STRIDE, PASTA, VAST), attack surface analysis, and industry standards (NIST, ISO 27001, MITRE ATT&CK) to understand security risks, identify vulnerabilities, assess threat actors and attack vectors, evaluate defensive controls, and recommend risk mitigation strategies.
17: 
18: ## When to Use This Skill
19: 
20: - **Security Incident Analysis**: Investigate breaches, data leaks, ransomware attacks, insider threats
21: - **Vulnerability Assessment**: Identify weaknesses in systems, applications, networks, processes
22: - **Threat Modeling**: Analyze potential attack vectors and threat actors for new systems or changes
23: - **Security Architecture Review**: Evaluate design decisions for security implications and gaps
24: - **Risk Assessment**: Quantify and prioritize security risks using frameworks like CVSS, FAIR
25: - **Compliance Analysis**: Assess adherence to security standards (SOC 2, PCI-DSS, HIPAA, GDPR)
26: - **Incident Response Planning**: Design detection, containment, eradication, and recovery strategies
27: - **Security Posture Evaluation**: Assess overall defensive capabilities and maturity
28: - **Code Security Review**: Identify security vulnerabilities in software implementations
29: 
30: ## Core Philosophy: Security Thinking
31: 
32: Cybersecurity analysis rests on fundamental principles:
33: 
34: **Defense in Depth**: No single security control is perfect. Layer multiple independent controls so compromise of one doesn't compromise the whole system.
35: 
36: **Assume Breach**: Modern security assumes attackers will penetrate perimeter defenses. Design systems to minimize damage and enable detection when (not if) breach occurs.
37: 
38: **Least Privilege**: Grant minimum access necessary for legitimate function. Every excess permission is an opportunity for exploitation.
39: 
40: **Zero Trust**: Never trust, always verify. Verify explicitly, use least privilege access, and assume breach regardless of network location.
41: 
42: **Security by Design**: Security cannot be bolted on afterward. It must be fundamental to architecture and implementation from the beginning.
43: 
44: **CIA Triad**: Security protects three properties—Confidentiality (only authorized access), Integrity (only authorized modification), Availability (accessible when needed).
45: 
46: **Threat-Informed Defense**: Base defensive priorities on understanding of actual threat actors, their capabilities, motivations, and tactics (threat intelligence).
47: 
48: **Risk-Based Approach**: Perfect security is impossible. Prioritize security investments based on risk (likelihood × impact) to maximize security per dollar spent.
49:

51: 
52: ## Theoretical Foundations (Expandable)
53: 
54: ### Foundation 1: CIA Triad (Classic Security Model)
55: 
56: **Components**:
57: 
58: **Confidentiality**: Information accessible only to authorized entities
59: 
60: - Protection mechanisms: Encryption, access controls, authentication
61: - Threats: Eavesdropping, data theft, unauthorized disclosure
62: - Example violations: Data breach, password theft, insider leak
63: 
64: **Integrity**: Information modifiable only by authorized entities in authorized ways
65: 
66: - Protection mechanisms: Hashing, digital signatures, access controls, version control
67: - Threats: Tampering, unauthorized modification, malware
68: - Example violations: Database manipulation, man-in-the-middle attacks, ransomware encryption
69: 
70: **Availability**: Information and systems accessible when needed by authorized entities
71: 
72: - Protection mechanisms: Redundancy, backups, DDoS mitigation, incident response
73: - Threats: Denial of service, ransomware, system destruction
74: - Example violations: DDoS attacks, ransomware, infrastructure failures
75: 
76: **Extensions**:
77: 
78: - **Authenticity**: Verified identity of entities and origin of information
79: - **Non-repudiation**: Cannot deny taking action
80: - **Accountability**: Actions traceable to entities
81: 
82: **Application**: Every security analysis should identify which aspects of CIA triad are at risk and how controls protect each.
83: 
84: **Sources**:
85: 
86: - [CIA Triad - Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_security#Key_concepts)
87: - [NIST Cybersecurity Framework](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework)
88: 
89: ### Foundation 2: Defense in Depth (Layered Security)
90: 
91: **Principle**: Deploy multiple layers of security controls so compromise of one layer doesn't compromise entire system.
92: 
93: **Historical Origin**: Military defensive strategy—multiple concentric perimeter defenses
94: 
95: **Security Layers**:
96: 
97: 1. **Physical**: Facility access controls, locked server rooms
98: 2. **Network**: Firewalls, network segmentation, IDS/IPS
99: 3. **Host**: Endpoint protection, host firewalls, patch management
100: 4. **Application**: Input validation, secure coding, authentication
101: 5. **Data**: Encryption at rest and in transit, DLP, tokenization
102: 6. **Human**: Security awareness training, phishing simulation
103: 
104: **Key Insight**: Redundancy is not waste—it's resilience. Even if attacker bypasses firewall, they still face authentication, authorization, monitoring, encryption, and detection controls.
105: 
106: **Application**: Security architecture should have multiple independent defensive layers protecting critical assets.
107: 
108: **Limitation**: Can create complexity and false sense of security if layers are not maintained or are interdependent.
109: 
110: **Sources**:
111: 
112: - [Defense in Depth - NSA](https://www.nsa.gov/Press-Room/Cybersecurity-Advisories-Guidance/)
113: - [Layered Security - CISA](https://www.cisa.gov/topics/cybersecurity-best-practices)
114: 
115: ### Foundation 3: Zero Trust Architecture
116: 
117: **Core Principle**: "Never trust, always verify" regardless of network location
118: 
119: **Contrast with Perimeter Model**: Traditional security assumed internal network is trusted ("castle and moat"). Zero trust assumes no network location is trusted.
120: 
121: **Key Tenets** (NIST SP 800-207):
122: 
123: 1. **Verify explicitly**: Always authenticate and authorize based on all available data points
124: 2. **Least privilege access**: Limit user access with Just-In-Time and Just-Enough-Access
125: 3. **Assume breach**: Minimize blast radius and segment access; verify end-to-end encryption
126: 
127: **Components**:
128: 
129: - **Identity-centric security**: Identity becomes new perimeter
130: - **Micro-segmentation**: Network divided into small zones with separate controls
131: - **Continuous verification**: Authentication and authorization are continuous, not one-time
132: - **Data-centric**: Protect data itself, not just perimeter around it
133: 
134: **Drivers**:
135: 
136: - Cloud adoption (no clear perimeter)
137: - Remote work (users outside traditional perimeter)
138: - Sophisticated attacks (perimeter breaches common)
139: 
140: **Application**: Modern security architectures should be designed with zero trust principles, especially for cloud and hybrid environments.
141: 
142: **Sources**:
143: 
144: - [NIST SP 800-207: Zero Trust Architecture](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-207/final)
145: - [Zero Trust - Microsoft Security](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/business/zero-trust)
146: 
147: ### Foundation 4: Threat Modeling
148: 
149: **Definition**: Structured approach to identify and prioritize potential threats to a system
150: 
151: **Purpose**: Proactively identify security issues during design phase when fixes are cheapest
152: 
153: **Benefits**:
154: 
155: - Find vulnerabilities before implementation
156: - Prioritize security work
157: - Communicate risks to stakeholders
158: - Guide security testing
159: 
160: **Common Methodologies**:
161: 
162: **STRIDE** (Microsoft):
163: 
164: - **S**poofing identity
165: - **T**ampering with data
166: - **R**epudiation
167: - **I**nformation disclosure
168: - **D**enial of service
169: - **E**levation of privilege
170: 
171: **PASTA** (Process for Attack Simulation and Threat Analysis):
172: 
173: - Seven-stage risk-centric methodology
174: - Aligns business objectives with technical requirements
175: 
176: **VAST** (Visual, Agile, and Simple Threat modeling):
177: 
178: - Scalable for agile development
179: - Two types: application threat models and operational threat models
180: 
181: **Application**: Use threat modeling for new features, architecture changes, or security reviews.
182: 
183: **Sources**:
184: 
185: - [Threat Modeling - OWASP](https://owasp.org/www-community/Threat_Modeling)
186: - [STRIDE Threat Model - Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/security/develop/threat-modeling-tool-threats)
187: 
188: ### Foundation 5: MITRE ATT&CK Framework
189: 
190: **Description**: Knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques based on real-world observations
191: 
192: **Purpose**: Understand how attackers operate to inform defense, detection, and threat hunting
193: 
194: **Structure**:
195: 
196: - **Tactics**: High-level goals (e.g., Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation)
197: - **Techniques**: Ways to achieve tactics (e.g., Phishing, Exploiting Public Applications)
198: - **Sub-techniques**: Specific implementations
199: - **Procedures**: Specific attacker behaviors
200: 
201: **14 Tactics** (Enterprise Matrix):
202: 
203: 1. Reconnaissance
204: 2. Resource Development
205: 3. Initial Access
206: 4. Execution
207: 5. Persistence
208: 6. Privilege Escalation
209: 7. Defense Evasion
210: 8. Credential Access
211: 9. Discovery
212: 10. Lateral Movement
213: 11. Collection
214: 12. Command and Control
215: 13. Exfiltration
216: 14. Impact
217: 
218: **Application**:
219: 
220: - Map defensive controls to ATT&CK techniques
221: - Identify detection gaps
222: - Threat intelligence sharing
223: - Red team/purple team exercises
224: 
225: **Value**: Common language for describing attacker behavior; basis for threat-informed defense
226: 
227: **Sources**:
228: 
229: - [MITRE ATT&CK](https://attack.mitre.org/)
230: - [ATT&CK Navigator](https://mitre-attack.github.io/attack-navigator/)
231:

234: ## Core Analytical Frameworks (Expandable)
235: 
236: ### Framework 1: Attack Surface Analysis
237: 
238: **Definition**: Identification and assessment of all points where unauthorized user could enter or extract data from system
239: 
240: **Components**:
241: 
242: **Attack Surface Elements**:
243: 
244: - **Network attack surface**: Exposed ports, services, protocols
245: - **Software attack surface**: Applications, APIs, web interfaces
246: - **Human attack surface**: Users, administrators, social engineering targets
247: - **Physical attack surface**: Facility access, hardware access
248: 
249: **Attack Vectors**: Methods attackers use to exploit attack surface
250: 
251: - Network-based: Port scanning, protocol exploits, man-in-the-middle
252: - Web-based: SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, authentication bypass
253: - Email-based: Phishing, malicious attachments, credential harvesting
254: - Physical: Theft, unauthorized access, evil maid attacks
255: - Social engineering: Pretexting, baiting, tailgating
256: 
257: **Analysis Process**:
258: 
259: 1. **Enumerate**: List all entry points and assets
260: 2. **Classify**: Categorize by type and criticality
261: 3. **Assess**: Evaluate exploitability and impact
262: 4. **Prioritize**: Rank by risk
263: 5. **Reduce**: Minimize unnecessary exposure
264: 
265: **Metrics**:
266: 
267: - Number of exposed services
268: - Number of internet-facing applications
269: - Number of privileged accounts
270: - Lines of code exposed to untrusted input
271: 
272: **Application**: Reducing attack surface is fundamental defensive strategy. Eliminate unnecessary exposure.
273: 
274: **Sources**:
275: 
276: - [Attack Surface Analysis - OWASP](https://owasp.org/www-community/Attack_Surface_Analysis_Cheat_Sheet)
277: - [Reducing Attack Surface - Microsoft](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/threat-protection/windows-defender-application-control/microsoft-recommended-block-rules)
278: 
279: ### Framework 2: Risk Assessment Frameworks
280: 
281: **Purpose**: Quantify and prioritize security risks to guide resource allocation
282: 
283: **Common Frameworks**:
284: 
285: **CVSS** (Common Vulnerability Scoring System):
286: 
287: - Standard for assessing vulnerability severity
288: - Score 0-10 based on exploitability, impact, scope
289: - Base score (intrinsic characteristics) + temporal + environmental scores
290: - Widely used but criticized for not capturing actual risk in specific contexts
291: 
292: **FAIR** (Factor Analysis of Information Risk):
293: 
294: - Quantitative risk framework
295: - Risk = Loss Event Frequency × Loss Magnitude
296: - Enables cost-benefit analysis of security investments
297: - More complex but provides dollar-denominated risk figures
298: 
299: **NIST Risk Management Framework** (RMF):
300: 
301: - Seven steps: Prepare, Categorize, Select, Implement, Assess, Authorize, Monitor
302: - Links security controls to risk management
303: - Used by U.S. federal agencies
304: 
305: **Qualitative vs. Quantitative**:
306: 
307: - **Qualitative**: High/Medium/Low risk ratings (simpler, faster, subjective)
308: - **Quantitative**: Numerical risk values (complex, objective, requires data)
309: 
310: **Application**: Risk assessment informs prioritization. Not all vulnerabilities are equally important—focus on highest risks.
311: 
312: **Sources**:
313: 
314: - [CVSS](https://www.first.org/cvss/)
315: - [FAIR Institute](https://www.fairinstitute.org/)
316: - [NIST RMF](https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/risk-management)
317: 
318: ### Framework 3: Security Control Frameworks
319: 
320: **Purpose**: Structured set of security controls to achieve security objectives
321: 
322: **Major Frameworks**:
323: 
324: **NIST Cybersecurity Framework**:
325: 
326: - Five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover
327: - Not prescriptive—flexible for different organizations
328: - Widely adopted across industries and internationally
329: 
330: **NIST SP 800-53** (Security and Privacy Controls):
331: 
332: - Comprehensive catalog of security controls for federal systems
333: - 20 control families (Access Control, Incident Response, etc.)
334: - Detailed implementation guidance
335: 
336: **CIS Controls** (Center for Internet Security):
337: 
338: - 18 prioritized security controls
339: - Implementation groups (IG1, IG2, IG3) based on organizational maturity
340: - Actionable and measurable
341: 
342: **ISO/IEC 27001**:
343: 
344: - International standard for information security management systems
345: - 14 control domains, 114 controls
346: - Certification available
347: 
348: **Application**: Use frameworks to:
349: 
350: - Ensure comprehensive coverage
351: - Benchmark security posture
352: - Communicate with stakeholders
353: - Meet compliance requirements
354: 
355: **Sources**:
356: 
357: - [NIST Cybersecurity Framework](https://www.nist.gov/cyberframework)
358: - [CIS Controls](https://www.cisecurity.org/controls)
359: - [ISO 27001](https://www.iso.org/isoiec-27001-information-security.html)
360: 
361: ### Framework 4: Incident Response Lifecycle
362: 
363: **Definition**: Structured approach to handling security incidents
364: 
365: **Standard Model** (NIST SP 800-61):
366: 
367: **Phase 1: Preparation**
368: 
369: - Establish IR capability, tools, playbooks
370: - Training and exercises
371: - Communication plans
372: 
373: **Phase 2: Detection and Analysis**
374: 
375: - Monitoring and alerting
376: - Incident classification and prioritization
377: - Initial investigation
378: - Scope determination
379: 
380: **Phase 3: Containment, Eradication, and Recovery**
381: 
382: - **Containment**: Stop spread (short-term and long-term)
383: - **Eradication**: Remove threat from environment
384: - **Recovery**: Restore systems to normal operation
385: 
386: **Phase 4: Post-Incident Activity**
387: 
388: - Lessons learned
389: - Evidence preservation
390: - Incident report
391: - Process improvement
392: 
393: **Key Concepts**:
394: 
395: - **Playbooks**: Predefined procedures for common incident types
396: - **Indicators of Compromise** (IoCs): Artifacts indicating malicious activity
397: - **Chain of custody**: Evidence handling procedures
398: - **Communication**: Internal and external stakeholders, legal, PR
399: 
400: **Metrics**:
401: 
402: - Mean Time to Detect (MTTD)
403: - Mean Time to Respond (MTTR)
404: - Mean Time to Contain (MTTC)
405: 
406: **Application**: Effective incident response minimizes damage, reduces recovery time, and captures learning.
407: 
408: **Sources**:
409: 
410: - [NIST SP 800-61: Computer Security Incident Handling Guide](https://csrc.nist.gov/publications/detail/sp/800-61/rev-2/final)
411: - [SANS Incident Response](https://www.sans.org/incident-response/)
412: 
413: ### Framework 5: Secure Development Lifecycle (SDL)
414: 
415: **Purpose**: Integrate security into software development process
416: 
417: **Microsoft SDL Phases**:
418: 
419: 1. **Training**: Security training for developers
420: 2. **Requirements**: Define security requirements and privacy requirements
421: 3. **Design**: Threat modeling, attack surface reduction, defense in depth
422: 4. **Implementation**: Secure coding standards, code analysis tools
423: 5. **Verification**: Security testing (SAST, DAST, penetration testing)
424: 6. **Release**: Final security review, incident response plan
425: 7. **Response**: Execute incident response plan if vulnerability discovered
426: 
427: **Key Practices**:
428: 
429: - **Static Analysis (SAST)**: Analyze source code for vulnerabilities
430: - **Dynamic Analysis (DAST)**: Test running application
431: - **Dependency Scanning**: Check third-party libraries for known vulnerabilities
432: - **Penetration Testing**: Simulate real attacks
433: - **Security Champions**: Embed security expertise in development teams
434: 
435: **OWASP SAMM** (Software Assurance Maturity Model):
436: 
437: - Maturity model for secure software development
438: - Five business functions: Governance, Design, Implementation, Verification, Operations
439: - Three maturity levels for each function
440: 
441: **Application**: Security must be integrated throughout development lifecycle, not just at the end.
442: 
443: **Sources**:
444: 
445: - [Microsoft SDL](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/securityengineering/sdl)
446: - [OWASP SAMM](https://owaspsamm.org/)
447:

449: 
450: ## Methodological Approaches (Expandable)
451: 
452: ### Method 1: Threat Intelligence Analysis
453: 
454: **Purpose**: Understand adversaries, their capabilities, tactics, and targets to inform defense
455: 
456: **Types of Threat Intelligence**:
457: 
458: **Strategic**: High-level trends for executives
459: 
460: - APT group activity and motivations
461: - Geopolitical cyber threats
462: - Industry-specific threat landscape
463: 
464: **Operational**: Campaign-level information for security operations
465: 
466: - Current attack campaigns
467: - Threat actor TTPs
468: - Malware families
469: 
470: **Tactical**: Technical indicators for immediate defense
471: 
472: - IP addresses, domains, file hashes
473: - YARA rules, Snort signatures
474: - CVEs being exploited
475: 
476: **Analytical Process**:
477: 
478: 1. **Collection**: Gather data from internal sources, threat feeds, OSINT, dark web
479: 2. **Processing**: Normalize, correlate, deduplicate
480: 3. **Analysis**: Contextualize, attribute, assess intent and capability
481: 4. **Dissemination**: Share with relevant teams in actionable format
482: 5. **Feedback**: Assess effectiveness and refine
483: 
484: **Frameworks**:
485: 
486: - **Diamond Model**: Adversary, Capability, Infrastructure, Victim
487: - **Kill Chain**: Reconnaissance → Weaponization → Delivery → Exploitation → Installation → C2 → Actions on Objectives
488: - **MITRE ATT&CK**: Map observed techniques to ATT&CK matrix
489: 
490: **Application**: Threat intelligence enables proactive, threat-informed defense rather than generic security measures.
491: 
492: **Sources**:
493: 
494: - [CISA Threat Intelligence](https://www.cisa.gov/topics/cyber-threats-and-advisories)
495: - [Threat Intelligence - SANS](https://www.sans.org/cyber-security-courses/cyber-threat-intelligence/)
496: 
497: ### Method 2: Penetration Testing
498: 
499: **Definition**: Authorized simulated attack to evaluate security of systems
500: 
501: **Types**:
502: 
503: **Black Box**: No prior knowledge (simulates external attacker)
504: 
505: **Gray Box**: Partial knowledge (simulates insider or compromised user)
506: 
507: **White Box**: Full knowledge (comprehensive security assessment)
508: 
509: **Phases** (Penetration Testing Execution Standard):
510: 
511: 1. **Pre-engagement**: Scope, rules of engagement, legal agreements
512: 2. **Intelligence gathering**: OSINT, network scanning, service enumeration
513: 3. **Threat modeling**: Identify potential attack vectors
514: 4. **Vulnerability analysis**: Identify exploitable weaknesses
515: 5. **Exploitation**: Attempt to exploit vulnerabilities
516: 6. **Post-exploitation**: Assess impact, lateral movement, privilege escalation
517: 7. **Reporting**: Document findings, demonstrate impact, provide remediation guidance
518: 
519: **Specialized Types**:
520: 
521: - **Web application penetration testing**: Focus on OWASP Top 10
522: - **Network penetration testing**: Internal and external network
